summary: Describes problems that hosts can have when a link has several IPv6 prefixes and the default address selection rules of RFC 3484 are used. Those rules have been hard to use in practice and can cause communication trouble. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you have several return addresses, picking the wrong one means replies get lost. This paper lists the trouble that can result.

questions: what is rfc 3484 default address selection
why does ipv6 pick the wrong source address
subtitle: A catalogue of ways a host with several IPv6 prefixes can pick the wrong address under the RFC 3484 default rules.

tldr.problem: A single link can carry several prefixes, so a host may have several addresses, and the default source and destination selection rules of RFC 3484 can pick one that causes dropped packets or failed connections.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through seven source address cases and three destination address cases, each with a short analysis of whether the RFC 3484 policy table can fix it or the rules need changing.
tldr.outcome: Most cases can be handled within the RFC 3484 framework by configuring a policy table, but doing that by hand on many hosts is impractical. The temporary address case cannot be solved that way.

today: RFC 5220 is an Informational problem statement, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes operational problems with the RFC 3484 default rules rather than specifying a new mechanism.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
In IPv6, one physical link can have multiple prefixes, so a host may have several addresses on one interface. This is typical in an IPv4-IPv6 dual-stack environment, or in a site connected to both a Unique Local Address (ULA) network and globally routable networks.

Choosing the wrong source address leads to unexpected asymmetric routing, filtering by a router, or discarded packets because there is no route back. Destination address selection matters too. RFC 3484 defines default source and destination selection algorithms implemented in a variety of OSs, but it has been too difficult to use operationally, partly because it lacks an autoconfiguration method.

The document focuses on end-site networks and unmanaged hosts, where behavior is hard to change by hand. Multihoming for redundancy is basically out of scope. Each case includes a brief solution analysis of whether the RFC 3484 framework can solve it.
sections.eli5: A computer with several addresses has to choose which one to write on each message. The default way it chooses does not always work well at home or in small offices.

sections.title: Source Address Problems: Routers and Filters
sections.content:
Three source address cases involve the network path.

  • Multiple routers on one interface. A host picks a source address with no interaction with next-hop choice, so it may send via Router1 using the address given by Router2. The analysis says controlling the host alone does not solve it; options are source-address-based routing at the routers, or static routing plus a matching static policy at the host.
  • Ingress filtering. A site with two upstream ISPs gets a prefix from each, usually a /48. A packet leaving through ISP2 with an ISP1 source address may be dropped by ISP2's ingress filter, which ISPs use to reduce the damage of denial-of-service attacks. Solutions are again source-address-based routing, or static routing plus a static host policy.
  • Half-closed network. One ISP link leads only to a closed network or VPN. Rule 8 (longest matching prefix) of RFC 3484 makes the host use the closed network's address even when talking to a host on the Internet, so the packet may be filtered and replies cannot return. This can be solved in the RFC 3484 framework by adding policy table entries.
sections.eli5: If two post offices each give you a stamp, the letter must carry the stamp from the post office it goes through, or it gets thrown away.

sections.title: Source Address Problems: ULA, Renumbering and More
sections.content:
Four more source cases concern the kind of address chosen.

  • Global and ULA together. Today the longest matching rule picks the correct address, because ULAs and global unicast addresses are dissimilar. If global unicast assignment later starts from 8000::/1, a destination such as 8000::1 would match the ULA fd01:2:3:100::100 for 1 bit but the global address for 0, so the wrong source would be chosen. Fixes are policy table entries or defining the ULA scope as smaller than global.
  • Site renumbering. Old prefixes take a long time to be invalidated, and RFC 4862 does not absolutely prohibit using a deprecated address for a new outgoing connection. A policy table can mitigate this.
  • Multicast source selection. A multicast packet crossing site borders should use a globally routable source, but longest match may choose a ULA.
  • Temporary addresses. Privacy addresses (RFC 3041) suit web browsing but are bad for address-based authentication and logging. This cannot be solved in the RFC 3484 framework; one possible answer is the socket API of RFC 5014, letting applications choose.
sections.eli5: Some of your addresses are only for use at home and some work everywhere. The default rule can mix them up, especially when you move house or want a disposable address for some things.

sections.title: Destination Address Problems
sections.content:
Three destination cases are described.

  • IPv4 or IPv6 first. The default policy table gives IPv6 higher precedence than IPv4. An administrator with native IPv4 but tunneled IPv6 may want the reverse, because the tunnel seems worse in quality. A policy table entry can do it.
  • ULA with IPv4 dual stack. An enterprise has IPv4 Internet access and only site-local IPv6 through a ULA. A host connecting to a server with both A and AAAA records picks the AAAA destination and the ULA source, which clearly fails. The policy table can solve it.
  • ULA or global first. Services are often differentiated by client source address (address-based authentication, internal pages, DNS zone splitting), but a ULA and a global address both have global scope and the RFC 3484 default rules do not say which wins. A policy table can solve it.
sections.eli5: When a friend has two phone numbers, you need a rule for which to call first. The built-in rule is not always the best one for your situation.

sections.title: Conclusion and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The root cause is that end hosts have multiple addresses and must choose both source and destination; routers alone cannot do this. Hosts must be informed about the routing policies of their upstream networks, and a site administrator must consider every possible false-selection problem and take countermeasures beforehand.

On security, policy routing combined with a bad address choice can send a packet to a VPN out over the Internet, which could allow eavesdropping or session hijack, though the RFC says these risks are not serious because returning the packet on the right path is not easy. Address selection can also expose privacy: an attacker who makes a host send a multicast packet may learn the ULAs attached to it. The RFC notes that choosing appropriate addresses avoids these risks.
sections.eli5: The lesson is that computers need to be told the house rules about which address to use, and that picking the wrong one can leak information too.
